# Oil Refining and Downstream — Deep Research Analysis (v3.8 R8)

Please conduct a systematic analysis of the following 8 global oil refining and downstream operators across 8 research dimensions.

## Entities

| # | Entity | Ticker |
|---|--------|--------|
| 1 | Marathon Petroleum | NYSE: MPC |
| 2 | Valero Energy | NYSE: VLO |
| 3 | Phillips 66 | NYSE: PSX |
| 4 | HF Sinclair | NYSE: DINO |
| 5 | PBF Energy | NYSE: PBF |
| 6 | Reliance Industries (O2C) | NSE: RELIANCE |
| 7 | S-Oil Corporation | KRX: 010950 |
| 8 | Sinopec (China Petroleum & Chemical) | SHA: 600028 |

## Research Dimensions

**Q1. Operable Crude Throughput Capacity — Consolidation Reconciliation**
For each entity, retrieve total crude refining capacity at the most recent fiscal year-end in thousand barrels per day (kbd), reported on an **operable basis net of idled units and equity-method JV pro-rata share** (not nameplate). For Reliance, separately disclose the Jamnagar SEZ vs DTA split; for Sinopec, reconcile consolidated capacity to equity-share capacity. State whether each figure is consolidated, equity-share, or capacity-share, and flag any restated prior-year figure.

**Q2. Refinery Footprint — Vintage Cohort & Geographic Concentration**
List each refinery by name, country/PADD region, and original commissioning year. Bucket assets into three vintage cohorts (<1970, 1970–2000, >2000) by share of total capacity. Compute a Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) of geographic concentration using kbd-weighted shares by region (PADD for US filers; state/province for Asian filers). Rank the eight entities from most to least geographically diversified.

**Q3. Refining Segment Revenue — Net of Eliminations, Per-Barrel & FX-Normalized**
Retrieve refining (or O2C/downstream) segment revenue for the most recent full fiscal year in USD millions, **net of intersegment eliminations**. For Reliance O2C, isolate the refining-attributable portion from petrochemicals using the company's product-mix disclosure; for Sinopec and S-Oil, convert from CNY/KRW using both period-average and period-end FX, and report the translation gap. Express each entity's refining revenue as $/barrel of throughput to one decimal place.

**Q4. Refining EBITDA Decomposition — Clean Cash Margin per Barrel**
For the most recent full fiscal year, decompose refining segment EBITDA into four components that reconcile to total: (a) crack-spread capture × throughput, (b) opex/bbl × throughput, (c) LIFO/FIFO inventory effect, (d) other (turnaround amortization, hedging, one-time items). Back out a "clean cash margin per barrel" comparable across US GAAP (LIFO) and IFRS (FIFO) filers. Additionally, compute a **counterfactual EBITDA** assuming crack spreads normalize to the trailing 5-year mid-cycle average, holding throughput and opex constant.

**Q5. System-Weighted Nelson Complexity & Complexity-Adjusted Margin**
For each entity, build a capacity-weighted Nelson Complexity Index (NCI) by individual refinery, disclosing the per-refinery NCI inputs and disclosure year. Where the company does not publish per-refinery NCI (likely Reliance, Sinopec, S-Oil), state the methodology used (e.g., regulator filings, third-party databases) and which sources were chosen and why. Compute "EBITDA per complexity-barrel" (Q4 clean cash margin ÷ system NCI) and rank entities.

**Q6. Utilization Rate — Reverse-Engineered & Downtime Decomposition**
Retrieve or reverse-engineer full-year refinery utilization (%) as actual throughput ÷ operable capacity (Q1 denominator). Where utilization is not directly disclosed (Reliance, Sinopec, S-Oil), compute it from throughput tables and document the calculation. Decompose lost capacity into (i) planned turnaround, (ii) unplanned outage, and (iii) economic run-cuts where the company discloses the split; otherwise state which disclosures are unavailable.

**Q7. Retail Footprint — Tiered Decomposition & Integration Depth**
Split each entity's branded retail station count into four tiers: company-operated, dealer/lessee, jobber/wholesale-supplied, and franchised. Note that PBF has no material retail footprint and that Reliance's retail is a JV with BP — handle each as a special case. Compute two integration ratios: (i) refining-capacity-to-retail-outlet (kbd per 1,000 stations) and (ii) implied throughput-per-station. Rank entities by downstream integration depth.

**Q8. Refining-Only Scope 1 Intensity — Equity vs Operational Control**
Retrieve Scope 1 GHG emissions in million tCO2e attributable to **refining only**, isolated from chemicals, midstream, and corporate. For integrated filers (Reliance O2C, Sinopec, PSX), document how the refining carve-out was performed. Report each entity on both equity-share and operational-control basis where both are disclosed, and state which the company uses by default. Normalize to (a) tCO2e per barrel of throughput and (b) tCO2e per complexity-weighted barrel (using Q5 system NCI). Identify the highest- and lowest-intensity operators and the principal driver of the gap.

# 64-Cell Reference Answers (Q1-Q8 parallel-built)

## Q1. Operable Crude Throughput Capacity — Consolidation Reconciliation

**Reporting basis.** All values are crude distillation (atmospheric) capacity at the most recent fiscal year-end, expressed as **operable** kbd (i.e., net of permanently idled or shutdown units and excluding announced-but-not-yet-effective closures unless explicitly noted). Equity-method JV interests are pro-rated; consolidated subsidiary capacity is taken at 100%. Today is 30-Apr-2026, so US filers' FY2025 10-Ks (filed Feb 2026), Sinopec's FY2025 A-share annual report (filed Mar 2026), Reliance's FY2025 (year-ended 31-Mar-2025) annual report, and S-Oil's FY2025 sustainability/business report are the primary sources.

### Narrative — Consolidation & ND-Treatment Notes

**Operable vs. nameplate.** US filers (MPC, VLO, PSX, DINO, PBF) report "throughput capacity" in 10-K Item 1 on what is effectively an operable basis — they do not include permanently shut units. The two live edge cases at FY2025YE:
- **VLO Benicia (145 kbd):** Idling announced Apr-2025; operations continued through 1Q26. FY25YE 10-K still includes it → reported 3,200 kbd; pro-forma post-idle 3,055 kbd disclosed in the same filing.
- **PSX Los Angeles (139 kbd):** Ceased crude processing in Q4-2025; **excluded** from FY25YE operable capacity → 10-K capacity table restated downward by 139 kbd vs. FY24.

**Equity-method handling.** Only PSX has a material equity-method refining JV (WRB Refining LP, 50% with Cenovus, covering Wood River 356 kbd and previously Borger — Borger is wholly-owned by PSX). FY25 net equity-share at Wood River = 178 kbd; combined with eight wholly-owned (Sweeny, Lake Charles, Bayway, Ferndale, Billings [divested 2023, exclude], Borger, Rodeo [now SAF/renewable], Humber-UK): renewable-converted Rodeo (San Francisco) crude capacity removed once converted; Humber UK 221 kbd is consolidated. Aggregating: Bayway 258 + Lake Charles 260 + Sweeny 265 + Borger 153 + Ferndale 105 + Humber 221 + Wood River (50%) 178 + Linden/Trainer-equivalent components → 1,608 kbd net, consistent with PSX 4Q25 fact sheet.

**Reliance SEZ vs DTA.** Reliance's audited disclosure is the **combined** Jamnagar number (~68.2 MMTPA ≈ 1,360–1,400 kbd). The SEZ refinery (commissioned 2008, export-oriented) and the DTA refinery (commissioned 1999) are not separately split in IFRS segment notes. The split shown is sourced from India's **PPAC (Petroleum Planning & Analysis Cell)** monthly refinery utilization reports — a Tier-1 regulator publication — yielding DTA 660 + SEZ 700 kbd. This is flagged as **ND-acceptable estimation via regulator filings**, with a ±20 kbd interval.

**Sinopec consolidated→equity reconciliation.** Sinopec's 268 MMTPA (≈5,360 kbd) consolidated figure assumes 100% of capacity at majority-owned subsidiaries. Pro-rating using the ownership-percentage schedule in the Annual Report (e.g., Shanghai Petrochemical 50.4%, Sinopec Shanghai Gaoqiao 100%, Fujian Refining JV 50%, BASF-YPC chemicals only) reduces the figure by an estimated ~180 kbd to ≈5,180 kbd equity-share. **Method:** Σ(subsidiary CDU capacity × Sinopec stake), with capacity by entity from the H-share 20-F equivalent (Stock Code 0386.HK) "Principal Operating Subsidiaries" note. Interval ±60 kbd reflects unallocated minor JV stakes.

**Restatement flags summary.** Two material restatements vs. prior-year disclosures: (1) PSX −139 kbd (LA shutdown); (2) PBF effective −50 kbd (Martinez fire de-rate, expected reversed in 2026). VLO carries a forward flag (Benicia). MPC, DINO, S-Oil, Reliance, Sinopec show no material YoY restatement of FY24 capacity.

**Source tier legend.** T1 = audited annual filing (10-K/20-F/Korea DART/CSRC); T2 = company investor presentation or earnings call; T3 = regulator (PPAC, EIA Refinery Capacity Report); T4 = third-party industry database (OGJ Worldwide Refining Survey, S&P Global Commodity Insights). Where company-audited disclosure is silent (Reliance SEZ/DTA split; Sinopec equity-share), T3/derived methods are explicitly cited.

## Q2. Refinery Footprint — Vintage Cohort & Geographic Concentration

**Methodology.** Refineries are listed by name, country/region (PADD for US filers; state/province for Asian filers; country for European JV plants). Original commissioning year ("vintage") is taken from the operator's most recent 10-K/20-F/annual report; where the filing only states "since 19XX," third-party industry databases (Oil & Gas Journal Worldwide Refining Survey 2024, S&P Global Commodity Insights Refinery Database) are used as **Tier-2** corroboration. HHI is computed as Σ(s_i)² where s_i is each region's share of system kbd (0–100 scale; max=10,000). Vintage cohort buckets are kbd-weighted, rounded to nearest 1%. ND ("non-disclosed") commissioning years are imputed from the earliest crude-unit start-up referenced in plant-history filings; flagged "[E]".

### Key narrative points

1. **Vintage skew.** US independents (MPC, VLO, PSX, DINO, PBF) operate almost entirely **pre-1970** asset bases — a function of the post-Clean-Air-Act greenfield drought. Net of capacity creep, **~85–100%** of their kbd was commissioned before 1970, with the only post-1970 greenfields being **Garyville (MPC, 1976)**, **Quebec (VLO, 1971)**, and selective expansions at **Corpus Christi (1983)**. No US Big-5 entity has any **>2000-vintage** crude unit.
2. **Asian post-2000 cohort dominance.** Reliance Jamnagar SEZ (2008) and Sinopec's Hainan (2006), Fujian-Quanzhou (2009), Zhongke-Zhanjiang (2020) push **>2000-vintage capacity** to ~47% (RIL) and ~20% (Sinopec) — materially newer than the US cohort, which has implications for Q5 (NCI) and Q8 (Scope-1 intensity).
3. **HHI floor cases.** Reliance and S-Oil each sit at the maximum HHI (10,000) by construction. For ranking purposes, they are reported tied at #7. A "site-level" HHI for Reliance (SEZ vs DTA) yields 5,005 if treated as separate operating units — disclosed for completeness but **not** used in the headline ranking, which follows the question's "state/province" instruction.
4. **Sinopec methodology note.** Sinopec does not publish a per-refinery kbd table in its annual report; capacity per site is taken from the **2024 Annual Report (H-share filing) p. 22–25** *plus* corroborating disclosures in subsidiary filings (e.g., Sinopec Shanghai 600688, Sinopec Yizheng) and **Argus China Petroleum 2024 Refinery Atlas** (Tier-3). Capacity-share treatment for Fujian (25% Saudi Aramco/ExxonMobil JV) follows Q1's equity-pro-rata convention.
5. **PBF Chalmette JV legacy.** Chalmette Refining was a 50/50 ExxonMobil-Venezuela JV until PBF's 2015 acquisition; it is now 100% PBF-consolidated. No equity-method adjustment required for FY24.

### Narrative

**Clean cash margin ranking (high→low, FY2025):** Reliance O2C ($18.3) ≫ S-Oil ($10.0) > VLO ($7.6) > MPC ($6.4) > PSX ($5.6) > DINO ($4.5) > PBF ($2.9) > Sinopec ($2.7).
Reliance's lead reflects (i) Jamnagar's NCI-14+ slate enabling deep heavy/sour discount capture, (ii) SEZ duty-free export economics, and (iii) cost-advantaged Indian opex. Sinopec sits at the bottom because the NDRC retail-price cap on diesel/gasoline truncates upside crack capture even when Singapore–Dubai widens.

**LIFO/FIFO comparability:** The four US LIFO filers reported a combined ~$1.0 B negative inventory effect (FY25 saw modest crude-price decline Q3→Q4). Stripping this restores ~$0.30/bbl across the LIFO cohort and is the dominant cross-standard adjustment. PSX (FIFO among US filers) shows a small positive inventory tailwind, structurally narrowing its reported-EBITDA gap to MPC/VLO when reverted to a clean basis.

**Opex/bbl dispersion** ($5.0 Reliance → $9.20 PBF) is the single largest driver of clean-margin spread after capture; PBF's Martinez/Paulsboro CA-cost stack and DINO's small-refinery overhead remain the structural laggards.

**Counterfactual at 5-yr mid-cycle:** Holding throughput/opex constant and applying entity-appropriate benchmark mid-cycles (USGC 3-2-1 ≈ $19/bbl; NWE Brent–ULSD ≈ $18/bbl; Singapore 92RON–Dubai ≈ $11/bbl), aggregate panel EBITDA contracts ~32%. PBF and Sinopec move closest to cash break-even; Reliance and S-Oil retain double-digit-billion / mid-single-digit-billion EBITDA respectively.

**ND-acceptable handling:**
- *Reliance:* Refining/petchem split inside O2C is **not separately reported in the audited segment note** (single O2C line). Estimate uses the company's quarterly product-volume mix table (Crude/Transport-fuels vs Polymers/Aromatics, IR deck slide ~14) prorated by external benchmark cracks vs olefin/aromatic margins; flagged **EST**.
- *Sinopec:* "Refining" segment as reported includes some intra-group product transfers; refining-only carve-out excludes Marketing & Distribution segment per Note 4(a). Inventory effect under IFRS uses weighted-average (no LIFO option in PRC GAAP/IFRS).
- *S-Oil:* Translation uses FY-avg KRW/USD 1,365 (BoK); FY-end translation gap noted in Q3 (period-end 1,398) is reported in Q3 only.

**Caveats:** All FY2025 figures for calendar-year filers reflect 10-K/20-F filings dated Feb–Apr 2026; Reliance's fiscal year ends 31-Mar-2026 (FY26 reporting) and is mapped to "FY2025" for cross-comparability. Intervals reflect (i) capture/bbl rounding in disclosed per-bbl statistics and (ii) segment-allocation discretion for integrated filers.

## Q5. System-Weighted Nelson Complexity Index (NCI) & Complexity-Adjusted Margin

**Scope/Convention.** NCI is a Solomon-Associates-derived ratio of conversion-unit capacity to atmospheric-distillation capacity. For each entity I compute a capacity-weighted system NCI (Σ kbd_i × NCI_i / Σ kbd_i) using the Q1 operable denominator. EBITDA / complexity-barrel = (Q4 clean cash margin, $/bbl) ÷ system NCI, expressed in $/(complexity-bbl). Where companies do not publish per-refinery NCI, I rely on (in priority): (1) Solomon Fuels Study peer-cell publications cited in 10-K/20-F, (2) IIR Energy / Wood Mackenzie refinery-by-refinery cards, (3) Oil & Gas Journal Worldwide Refining Survey (annual), (4) regulator filings (CARB, EPA RMP, India PNGRB, KRX disclosures). - **Reliance (T3 + T1 composite, ND-acceptable):** Reliance does not disclose per-stream NCI for SEZ vs DTA. The 21.1 figure quoted in AR FY24 (p.84) is the *integrated O2C* complexity (refining + aromatics + olefins). For a refining-only NCI I split Jamnagar into SEZ (heavy-feed, deep-conversion: coker + RFCC + alky + ARU + ISOM ⇒ NCI≈14.0) and DTA (FCC + delayed coker, ARU ⇒ NCI≈11.3) using IIR Asia 2024 stream-level card, cross-checked against PNGRB capacity register. Estimation method = unit-credit reconstruction (Solomon factors × disclosed CDU/VDU/FCC/HCU/Coker capacities in AR). Interval width reflects ±1 NCI point on the SEZ side.
- **S-Oil (T3, ND-acceptable):** Single-site, so weighting is trivial. NCI from Wood Mackenzie 2024 (12.7) and OGJ Worldwide Refining Survey Dec-2024 (12.5). - **Sinopec (T3/T4, ND-acceptable):** Sinopec's 2024 20-F (p.45–47) discloses total processing capacity but no per-site NCI. Wood Mackenzie China Downstream Service 2024 + IEA *Oil 2024* dataset provide refinery-level NCI estimates; for ~12 listed sites I used WoodMac directly and for the residual (~36% of throughput across smaller plants) applied an average NCI of 7.0 (consistent with Chinese sector mean per CNPC ETRI 2023). The interval (7.3–8.3) reflects this residual assumption.

### Why the gap between best and worst is *not* purely complexity

The complexity-adjusted margin compresses the visible US-vs-Asia margin gap considerably (raw clean-margin ratio MPC/Sinopec ≈ 2.5×, but per-complexity-bbl ratio is only ~1.6×). Yet US Gulf Coast operators (MPC, VLO) still dominate the ranking because: (i) discounted heavy/sour crude slates exploit their high coking/HDS share; (ii) RFS RIN economics monetize complexity that Asian peers cannot capture; (iii) Sinopec carries policy-driven product-slate and crude-procurement constraints that depress capture even on equally complex units. PBF has the highest system NCI (12.9) but its captured margin — particularly post-Martinez fire 2025 — does not scale linearly, illustrating that NCI is a *capability* metric, not a *capture* metric.

### Methodology & Reverse-Engineering Notes (per ND-acceptable handling)

**MPC, VLO, PSX, DINO, PBF.** All five US filers directly disclose throughput-by-region tables in their 10-K MD&A and a utilization percentage in 4Q earnings releases. Utilization is reported by MPC and VLO as "crude capacity utilization" explicitly; PSX/DINO/PBF disclose throughput and capacity separately and analyst calculation = throughput ÷ capacity. Planned vs unplanned splits are partially disclosed: MPC and VLO discuss turnaround impact in MD&A in pp-of-throughput terms (Item 7 — "Factors affecting comparability"); economic run-cuts are rarely quantified except by PSX (Rodeo conversion is structural, not cyclical run-cut) and PBF (Martinez extended outage classification disputed in 10-K Item 1A risk factor).

**Reliance Industries (O2C).** RIL does **not** publish a refinery utilization ratio. Reverse-engineering uses two anchors: (i) PPAC monthly "Refinery Production" file, which lists Jamnagar SEZ + DTA crude processed in MMT, converted to kbd at 7.33 bbl/MT and divided by 365; (ii) RIL Integrated Annual Report O2C section, which gives total feedstock processed (crude + condensate + other). The denominator is operable capacity, which exceeds the 1,360 kbd nameplate by ~5–7% due to ongoing debottlenecks — RIL has historically reported run rates >100% of nameplate. We therefore present the figure on **both nameplate and operable bases**; benchmark answer uses operable. Planned/unplanned/economic decomposition is **not disclosed** — flagged as data gap.

**S-Oil.** Korean filers report 가동률 (utilization rate) in the Business Report (사업보고서) Section II, by business unit (정유, 윤활기유, 석유화학). The 정유 (refining) figure is published as a percentage; cross-checked against Onsan crude runs from KPX and KNOC monthly trade data. Planned downtime tied to Shaheen Project tie-ins (steam cracker integration) is referenced qualitatively in MD&A but not quantified in pp.

**Sinopec.** No utilization percentage published. Reverse-engineering: numerator = "原油加工量" (crude throughput) in Mt from Annual Report Refining Segment table (FY2025 ≈ 251 Mt = ~5,020 kbd at 7.33 bbl/MT ÷ 365); denominator = consolidated nameplate of ~5,540 kbd (305 Mt) reconciled in Q1. Equity-share utilization assumes the same ratio applied to the ~5,000 kbd equity capacity (minor delta because most refining is wholly-owned). Sinopec **does** explicitly discuss economic run-cuts: 1H25 Results Announcement p.12 ("我们 optimized refinery utilization given the persistent weakness in domestic gasoline/diesel demand and the tightening of fuel oil export quotas") — material driver in 2025, distinguishing Sinopec from US peers whose lost capacity is dominated by turnaround/unplanned events.

### Cross-entity observations

- **Highest utilization:** MPC (95.4%) and S-Oil (95.7%); both benefit from low planned-outage years and strong export pull.
- **Lowest utilization:** PBF (83.1%) — Martinez fire-driven; structural rather than economic.
- **Economic run-cuts as a meaningful component** are concentrated at **Sinopec** (domestic demand softness, fuel-oil export quota tightening) and **PSX** (Rodeo wind-down, LA Refinery closure); for US Gulf Coast and Asian export refiners (RIL, S-Oil), economic curtailment is immaterial in FY2025.
- **Disclosure gap:** Three of eight entities (RIL, S-Oil, Sinopec) do not publish a utilization percentage, requiring reverse-engineering. None of the eight publishes a clean three-way (planned / unplanned / economic) lost-barrel waterfall — typical splits are derived from MD&A narrative, 8-K incident filings (PBF Martinez 2/2025; MPC Martinez 11/2023 residual), and cross-reference to industry T/A databases (IIR, Wood Mackenzie). This is flagged per cell in the table.

### Source tier summary

T1 (regulatory filing) used as primary for all US filers and Sinopec A-share annual report; T2 (earnings release / IR deck) used for quarterly granularity and S-Oil; T3 (regulator/3rd-party) used as cross-check for RIL (PPAC), Sinopec (NEA) and S-Oil (KPX). No cell relies solely on T3.

### Narrative

**Scope of Q8.** Only combustion + process emissions from crude distillation, conversion (FCC, hydrocracking, coking), hydrotreating, hydrogen production, utilities, and on-site cogen serving the refinery fence are counted. Petrochemicals, lubes/base-oil units (where physically separable), midstream pipelines/terminals, retail, corporate offices, and Scope 2 imported power are excluded. Where cogen exports steam/power off-site, the gross "as-emitted" figure is retained (operational-control convention) rather than allocated.

**Equity vs. Operational-Control basis.** Five of the eight (MPC, VLO, DINO, PBF, S-Oil) operate substantially all assets directly and report on an operational-control basis only — equity and OC values converge. **PSX is the principal exception**: it discloses both, with equity-share Scope 1 (~19.4 Mt) materially higher than OC (~17.1 Mt) because of the WRB Refining JV (50% with Cenovus, operated by PSX) and the formerly-50% Borger asset; it defaults to OC for headline metrics but publishes the equity reconciliation in the Climate Data Sheet. **Reliance** reports BRSR Scope 1 on operational control only; equity-share would be modestly lower because the Sikka terminal and certain utilities are JVs. **Sinopec** reports Group Scope 1 on a consolidated/operational-control basis under China's MEE methodology; equity-share is not separately published — the gap is material because Sinopec consolidates several majority-owned but not 100%-held refineries (e.g., Yangzi, Hainan).

**Carve-out methodology for integrated filers.**
- **PSX:** Direct segment disclosure ("Refining" line in Climate Data Sheet) — Tier 1.
- **Reliance O2C:** No published refining/petchem split. Reference answer uses an **energy-allocation method**: 48% of consolidated O2C Scope 1 is assigned to refining, derived from FY24 feedstock-MJ shares disclosed in the Integrated Annual Report (refining throughput × LHV vs. petchem feed × LHV). A throughput-only allocation (Tier 3 sensitivity) yields ~26 Mt; the 19.5–24.5 Mt interval brackets both methods.
- **Sinopec:** No segment Scope 1 split. Allocation uses the China refining sector energy-intensity factor (≈ 73 kg CO₂e/bbl per CNPC ETRI 2023, scaled to Sinopec throughput) cross-checked against the consolidated total. The interval (82–95 Mt) reflects the spread between bottom-up (throughput × benchmark intensity = 88 Mt) and top-down (54% sector-energy share of consolidated 165 Mt = 89 Mt).
- **S-Oil:** Onsan complex is integrated refining + lubes + petchem (RUC/ODC). Carve-out via CDP C6.1 process emissions disaggregation, scaled by capacity utilization.

**Highest and lowest intensity operators.**
- **Highest tCO₂e/bbl: Sinopec at 0.049** — driven by (i) older, lower-complexity sites (system NCI ~10.8) requiring more thermal duty per unit upgrading, (ii) heavier reliance on coal/refinery-fuel-gas with high CF in utilities, and (iii) a higher share of bottom-of-barrel conversion (delayed coking) versus pure hydroskimming. **Reliance** ranks second at 0.043 because Jamnagar's deep-conversion configuration (NCI 21.1) burns substantial fuel for hydrocracking/H₂; however, on a *complexity-adjusted* basis Reliance is among the **lowest at 0.00204 t/complexity-bbl**, reflecting modern thermal integration.
- **Lowest tCO₂e/bbl: MPC at 0.0244**, followed closely by PSX (0.0259) and VLO (0.0274) — reflecting Gulf Coast scale, gas-fired utilities, and recent efficiency capex. On a complexity-adjusted basis, **PSX (0.00207)** and **Reliance (0.00204)** are the most efficient per complexity-barrel; **Sinopec (0.00454)** remains the highest by a wide margin.

**Principal driver of the gap.** ~70% of the spread between Sinopec/Reliance and the US Gulf cohort is fuel-mix and utility-CF (refinery fuel gas + natural gas in the US vs. blended FG/coal-cogen in Asia); the residual ~30% reflects complexity-driven hydrogen demand and turnaround-cycle thermal losses. Operational-vs-equity reframing changes PSX rank by one position (worsens to 0.0294 t/bbl on equity basis) but does not alter the head/tail of the distribution.

9. **Fabricated franchised tier** for entities where the model is not used (MPC, VLO, PSX, DINO, Reliance, S-Oil all = 0 franchised) → cap that cell at **0.25**.

### Cross-Cutting Penalties (Q8-specific)

- **Citation missing entirely** for any cell → caps that cell at **0.5**, regardless of numeric accuracy.
- **Integrated-filer carve-out trap** (PSX, Reliance, Sinopec): if no carve-out method is stated for these three cells, cap at **0.5**; if the response simply uses consolidated/group Scope 1 as if it were refining, cap at **0.25**.
- **ND-with-no-method**: where the company does not publish refining-only or equity-share Scope 1 (Reliance refining split, Sinopec refining split, Sinopec equity-share, S-Oil refining split) and the response provides a number without naming the allocation method (energy-share, throughput × benchmark intensity, CDP disaggregation, etc.) → cap at **0.25**.
- **Equity vs. OC framing trap** (PSX): failing to disclose both bases when PSX publishes both, or failing to identify OC as the default → drop one tier on the PSX cell.
- **Normalization completeness**: missing **either** tCO₂e/bbl **or** tCO₂e/complexity-bbl drops the cell one tier; missing both caps at **0.25**.
- **NCI cross-link integrity**: complexity-adjusted figure must use the entity's Q5 system NCI; using a generic 10.0 or industry average without flagging → drop one tier.
- **Highest/lowest identification**: response that fails to identify Sinopec as highest-intensity and MPC (or PSX-tied) as lowest, **and** fails to articulate the fuel-mix/utility-CF + complexity driver of the gap → drop one tier on the overall narrative-dependent cells (does not affect numeric cells already scored).
- **Unit/scope confusion**: mixing Scope 1+2 or including Scope 3 inadvertently → cap at **0.25** for that cell; reporting in tons rather than Mt without conversion → drop one tier.

# Oil Refining and Downstream — Deep Research Analysis (v3.8 R8)

**Critical Methodological Disclosure:** This analysis synthesizes publicly disclosed data through fiscal year 2023 (with FY2024 data where available for US filers reporting on calendar-year basis). Several requested decompositions — particularly Q4's four-way EBITDA bridge, Q6's downtime taxonomy, and Q7's four-tier retail split — exceed the granularity that most of these issuers publicly disclose. Where I cannot source a number directly, I state the gap rather than fabricate. Per-refinery Nelson Complexity Index values for Asian operators are particularly opaque and rely on third-party estimates.

---

## Q1. Operable Crude Throughput Capacity

| Entity | Capacity (kbd) | Basis | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Marathon Petroleum | ~2,950 | Consolidated, operable | 13 refineries; reflects post-Martinez conversion (renewable diesel) |
| Valero Energy | ~3,200 | Consolidated, operable | 15 refineries (US, Canada, UK); excludes idled units |
| Phillips 66 | ~1,800 (FY24); ~1,900 (FY23) | Net pro-rata equity share | Reflects Rodeo conversion to renewables (closed Feb 2024) and 50% WRB JV share; Alliance idled (Hurricane Ida) excluded |
| HF Sinclair | ~678 | Consolidated, operable | 7 refineries post-Sinclair merger (2022) |
| PBF Energy | ~1,000 | Consolidated, operable | 6 refineries; Martinez restored after 2025 fire (FY24 reflected partial outage) |
| Reliance O2C (Jamnagar) | ~1,360 total: SEZ ~704 + DTA ~660 | Consolidated | Single-site complex; capacity sometimes quoted as 1.4 MMbd nameplate |
| S-Oil | ~669 | Consolidated | Single Onsan refinery |
| Sinopec | Consolidated ~5,080; equity-share ~4,900 | Both shown | ~245 MMt/yr crude run capacity ≈ 5.08 MMbd; minor adjustments for non-wholly-owned refineries (e.g., BASF-YPC, Fujian JV) |

**Restatements flagged:** PSX restated FY22/FY23 capacity downward following Rodeo conversion. MPC restated post-Martinez conversion. Sinopec capacity drifts ±2% YoY with minor debottlenecking; reconciliation between Chinese metric tonnes and bpd uses ~7.33 bbl/t conversion typical of medium sour crude slate.

---

## Q2. Refinery Footprint — Vintage & Geographic Concentration

**Vintage cohort distribution (capacity-weighted, approximate):**

| Entity | <1970 | 1970–2000 | >2000 |
|---|---|---|---|
| MPC | ~55% | ~40% | ~5% (debottlenecking) |
| VLO | ~50% | ~45% | ~5% |
| PSX | ~60% | ~35% | ~5% |
| DINO | ~70% | ~25% | ~5% |
| PBF | ~65% | ~35% | 0% |
| Reliance | 0% | ~50% (1999 phase 1) | ~50% (2008 phase 2) |
| S-Oil | 0% | 100% (1980, 1991, 1997 expansions) | RUC/ODC 2018 |
| Sinopec | ~20% | ~50% | ~30% (post-2000 capacity adds dominate) |

**Regional concentration (HHI on kbd-weighted shares):**

- **MPC:** PADD II ~35%, PADD III ~40%, PADD V ~15%, PADD IV ~10% → HHI ≈ 3,150
- **VLO:** PADD III ~55%, PADD V ~15%, PADD II ~10%, non-US ~20% → HHI ≈ 3,750
- **PSX:** PADD III ~35%, PADD V ~25%, PADD II ~20%, PADD I ~10%, EU ~10% → HHI ≈ 2,450
- **DINO:** PADD IV ~50%, PADD III ~35%, PADD V ~15% → HHI ≈ 3,950
- **PBF:** PADD I ~40%, PADD V ~40%, PADD III ~20% → HHI ≈ 3,600
- **Reliance:** Gujarat 100% → HHI = 10,000
- **S-Oil:** South Gyeongsang 100% → HHI = 10,000
- **Sinopec:** Top provinces (Shandong, Guangdong, Jiangsu, Hubei, Fujian) each 10–20% → HHI ≈ 1,400

**Diversification ranking (most to least diversified):**
1. Sinopec → 2. PSX → 3. MPC → 4. PBF → 5. VLO → 6. DINO → 7. Reliance → 8. S-Oil

---

## Q3. Refining Segment Revenue — Per-Barrel & FX-Normalized

FY2023 figures (USD M, net of intersegment eliminations):

| Entity | Refining Revenue ($M) | Throughput (MMbbl) | $/bbl |
|---|---|---|---|
| MPC | ~135,000 | ~1,000 | ~135.0 |
| VLO | ~135,000 | ~1,100 | ~122.7 |
| PSX (Refining segment) | ~115,000 | ~660 | ~174.2 |
| DINO (Refining segment) | ~25,500 | ~225 | ~113.3 |
| PBF | ~38,300 | ~330 | ~116.1 |
| Reliance O2C (refining-attributable carve-out) | ~55,000 (of ~73B total O2C) | ~500 | ~110.0 |
| S-Oil | ~27,500 (USD-converted) | ~225 | ~122.2 |
| Sinopec (Refining segment, USD) | ~225,000 | ~1,830 | ~122.9 |

**FX translation gaps (Sinopec, S-Oil):**
- Sinopec FY23: CNY avg 7.08, period-end 7.10 → translation gap <0.5%
- S-Oil FY23: KRW avg 1,306, period-end 1,288 → ~1.4% translation gap; period-end conversion yields ~$28.0B vs ~$27.5B at average

**Reliance O2C carve-out methodology:** Reliance does not split refining and petrochemicals in segment reporting post-2020. Carve-out applied product-mix ratios from physical throughput disclosures (~75% of O2C volume is refined product) and a refining gross margin proxy from the Singapore complex margin.

---

## Q4. Refining EBITDA Decomposition — Clean Cash Margin per Barrel

FY2023 refining segment EBITDA (USD B) and approximate decomposition. **Caveat:** Only US filers (LIFO) explicitly disclose inventory effects; the four-way bridge below uses approximations from MD&A for the (a)/(b) split, with (c)/(d) computed by reconciliation residual.

| Entity | EBITDA ($B) | Throughput (MMbbl) | Implied $/bbl | LIFO/FIFO note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MPC | ~14.5 | ~1,000 | ~14.5 | LIFO; ~$0 inventory effect FY23 |
| VLO | ~13.5 | ~1,100 | ~12.3 | LIFO |
| PSX (Refining) | ~5.5 | ~660 | ~8.3 | LIFO; Rodeo charges noisy |
| DINO | ~2.4 | ~225 | ~10.7 | LIFO |
| PBF | ~2.6 | ~330 | ~7.9 | LIFO |
| Reliance O2C (refining-attributable) | ~6.5 | ~500 | ~13.0 | FIFO (IFRS) |
| S-Oil | ~1.7 | ~225 | ~7.6 | Weighted-avg (IFRS) |
| Sinopec Refining | ~9.0 | ~1,830 | ~4.9 | Weighted-avg; subject to ceiling-price effects |

**Clean cash margin per barrel (LIFO→FIFO normalized):** MPC ~$14.5, VLO ~$12.3, Reliance ~$13.0, DINO ~$10.7, PSX ~$8.3, PBF ~$7.9, S-Oil ~$7.6, Sinopec ~$4.9.

**Counterfactual EBITDA at mid-cycle cracks (5Y avg ~$15/bbl 3:2:1 vs FY23 ~$25/bbl):** Apply ~40% margin compression to crack-spread component. Implied normalized EBITDA: MPC ~$8–9B, VLO ~$8B, PSX ~$3B, DINO ~$1.4B, PBF ~$1.4B, Reliance ~$4B, S-Oil ~$1B, Sinopec ~$5–6B (Chinese pricing mechanism partially insulates from cracks but caps upside).

**Disclosure gap:** None of the eight publish a clean four-way bridge; (c) and (d) are inferable only for US LIFO filers.

---

## Q5. System-Weighted Nelson Complexity Index

| Entity | System NCI (cap-weighted) | Source | Clean margin $/bbl | $/complexity-bbl |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MPC | ~11.0 | Company 10-K disclosures | 14.5 | 1.32 |
| VLO | ~12.0 | Company filings | 12.3 | 1.03 |
| PSX | ~12.5 | Company filings | 8.3 | 0.66 |
| DINO | ~12.0 | Company filings (HF legacy) | 10.7 | 0.89 |
| PBF | ~12.8 | Company filings; high due to Chalmette/Toledo/Paulsboro | 7.9 | 0.62 |
| Reliance | ~21.1 (Jamnagar industry-cited) | Company investor presentations + OGJ | 13.0 | 0.62 |
| S-Oil | ~10.5 | Industry estimates (KPC, OGJ); company does not publish | 7.6 | 0.72 |
| Sinopec | ~7–8 (estimate) | Third-party: Wood Mackenzie, OGJ Worldwide Refining Survey | 4.9 | ~0.65 |

**Methodology for non-disclosing operators:** S-Oil and Sinopec do not publish per-refinery NCI. Used OGJ Worldwide Refining Survey (annual) and Wood Mackenzie refinery database, cross-checked against unit-by-unit hydrocracker/coker capacity disclosed in sustainability reports. Reliance's 21.1 figure is widely cited from company communications but is not unit-decomposed publicly.

**Ranking by EBITDA per complexity-barrel:** MPC > VLO > DINO > S-Oil > PSX > Sinopec ≈ Reliance ≈ PBF.

**Interpretation:** High Reliance NCI dilutes its $/complexity-bbl despite strong absolute margin — the complexity is a moat against feed/product flexibility rather than a current-cycle margin driver.

---

## Q6. Utilization Rate — Reverse-Engineered

FY2023 (FY24 where reported):

| Entity | Throughput (kbd) | Op. Capacity (kbd) | Utilization | Downtime split |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MPC | ~2,740 | ~2,950 | ~93% | Discloses planned turnaround impact aggregate; unplanned not separated |
| VLO | ~3,015 | ~3,200 | ~94% | Discloses planned vs unplanned in MD&A narrative |
| PSX | ~1,810 | ~1,900 (FY23) | ~95% | Aggregate disclosure only |
| DINO | ~620 | ~678 | ~92% | Salt Lake City fire (FY23) disclosed |
| PBF | ~905 | ~1,000 | ~91% | Toledo and Martinez incidents disclosed |
| Reliance | ~1,400 (~102% nameplate use is typical) | ~1,360 op. | ~100%+ | No formal split; SEZ runs ahead of nameplate |
| S-Oil | ~609 | ~669 | ~91% | RUC turnarounds disclosed in earnings calls |
| Sinopec | ~5,015 (~250 MMt run) | ~5,080 | ~99% | No split published |

**Decomposition gap:** None of the eight provide a clean (i)/(ii)/(iii) split. US filers occasionally disclose turnaround days; economic run-cuts are virtually never disclosed quantitatively. Sinopec utilization >95% reflects state-directed product supply rather than economic optimization.

---

## Q7. Retail Footprint — Tiered Decomposition

| Entity | Co-op | Dealer/Lessee | Jobber/Wholesale | Franchise | Total | Special note |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MPC | ~0 (post-Speedway sale to 7-Eleven 2021) | ~0 | ~7,000 (Marathon-branded jobbers) | 0 | ~7,000 | Wholesale-only model post-Speedway |
| VLO | ~0 | ~1,000 | ~6,000 | 0 | ~7,000 | Mostly jobber-supplied; CST Brands divested |
| PSX | ~0 | ~600 (76, Conoco direct-served) | ~7,000 | ~500 (JET in Europe) | ~8,000+ | Marketing arm spans US/EU |
| DINO | ~310 (Sinclair-operated) | ~1,300 | ~1,000 | 0 | ~2,600 | Sinclair brand restored licensee model |
| PBF | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | No material retail (special case) |
| Reliance | ~1,500 (own + JV with BP "Jio-bp") | 0 | 0 | 0 | ~1,500 | JV; BP holds 49% of retail JV |
| S-Oil | ~2,100 | ~0 | 0 | 0 | ~2,100 | Mostly company-leased; Aramco supplied |
| Sinopec | ~30,000+ (Sinopec gas stations; partial co-op) | ~0 | 0 | ~0 | ~30,000+ | Largest retail network globally; mostly direct-operated |

**Integration ratios:**

| Entity | kbd / 1,000 stations | Implied throughput per station (bbl/yr) |
|---|---|---|
| MPC | 421 | ~143,000 |
| VLO | 457 | ~157,000 |
| PSX | 225 | ~83,000 |
| DINO | 261 | ~87,000 |
| PBF | n/a | n/a |
| Reliance | 907 | ~340,000 (export-heavy; retail underweights) |
| S-Oil | 319 | ~106,000 |
| Sinopec | 169 | ~61,000 |

**Downstream integration depth ranking** (combining station density and refining-supply ratio): Sinopec > PSX > S-Oil > DINO > MPC ≈ VLO > Reliance > PBF. Reliance has high refining capacity per station because Jamnagar is export-oriented; integration is structurally shallower than the network suggests.

---

## Q8. Refining-Only Scope 1 Intensity

FY2023 disclosures (refining-only carve-out, MtCO2e):

| Entity | Scope 1 Refining (Mt) | Basis disclosed | tCO2e/bbl | tCO2e/complexity-bbl |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MPC | ~36 | Operational control (default) | 0.036 | 0.0033 |
| VLO | ~33 | Operational control | 0.030 | 0.0025 |
| PSX | ~17 (refining only) | Operational + equity in sustainability supplement | 0.026 | 0.0021 |
| DINO | ~6.5 | Operational | 0.029 | 0.0024 |
| PBF | ~9 | Operational | 0.027 | 0.0021 |
| Reliance O2C (refining carve-out) | ~28 (estimated; total O2C ~45) | Operational; no clean refining/chem split published | 0.056 | 0.0027 |
| S-Oil | ~9 | Operational | 0.040 | 0.0038 |
| Sinopec (Refining segment) | ~75 (estimated from group ~190 Mt apportioned) | Operational only | 0.041 | ~0.0055 |

**Carve-out methodology for integrated filers:**
- **PSX:** Sustainability report splits Refining vs Midstream vs Chemicals (CPChem JV); used Refining-only line.
- **Reliance:** O2C aggregates refining + petchem; apportioned 60/40 to refining based on energy intensity ratios in BRSR filing.
- **Sinopec:** Group-level Scope 1 disclosure; refining-only inferred from segment fuel/energy consumption disclosed in CSR report (~40% of total).

**Equity vs operational control:** Only PSX and Reliance disclose both bases for non-wholly-owned assets (WRB JV, BP retail JV); the rest report operational control only.

**Highest intensity:** Reliance (0.056 tCO2e/bbl absolute). **Lowest:** PSX (0.026). **Principal driver of the gap:** Crude slate heaviness and hydrogen-intensity. Reliance's NCI 21+ requires very large hydrogen production (steam methane reforming = principal Scope 1 contributor) and processes heavy/sour crudes. PSX's lower intensity reflects lighter-crude PADD III/V slates and the renewable conversion of Rodeo, which removed a hydrogen-intensive heavy-crude unit from the operational-control denominator. On a complexity-adjusted basis (tCO2e/complexity-bbl), the dispersion narrows substantially — Reliance moves to mid-pack — confirming that complexity, not operational efficiency, drives most of the absolute-intensity gap.

---

### Summary Limitations

1. **Q4 four-way EBITDA bridge** is not publicly reconcilable for any of the eight; values are best-estimate.
2. **Q5 NCI** for S-Oil and Sinopec relies on third-party databases (OGJ, Wood Mackenzie); company-disclosed values are not available at refinery level.
3. **Q6 downtime taxonomy** is not disclosed in the requested (i)/(ii)/(iii) split by any operator.
4. **Q7 four-tier retail split** uses approximations; modern wholesale models blur dealer vs jobber distinctions.
5. **Q8 refining-only Scope 1** carve-outs for Reliance and Sinopec are analytical apportionments, not directly disclosed.

Where exact figures matter for downstream use (e.g., investment committee, M&A diligence), each line item should be re-sourced to the underlying 10-K, 20-F, integrated annual report, or sustainability supplement.

Q1.rationale: Several headline capacities are directionally close, but the answer uses stale FY2023/FY2024 framing, lacks specific citations, and misses key FY2025 reconciliation flags such as PSX LA shutdown and PBF Martinez de-rate. Reliance and Sinopec include useful splits/bases but without the required regul

Q2.rationale: Most HHI and vintage cohort values are materially wrong, with no refinery-by-refinery commissioning list or citations. The single-site Reliance and S-Oil cases are mostly recognized, but Sinopec, Valero, DINO, and PBF are far outside reference HHI bands.

Q3.rationale: The answer uses FY2023 rather than the benchmark FY2024 values, has no segment-note citations, and omits required dual-rate FX treatment for Reliance. Sinopec reports only the gross view and S-Oil is substantially wrong on revenue and per-barrel metrics.

Q4.rationale: The EBITDA and clean-margin values are largely FY2023 cycle-peak figures and are far from the FY2025 reference, with no true four-component reconciliation. Only limited directionality is present for the Asian carve-outs and Sinopec price-cap discussion.

Q5.rationale: Most system NCI estimates are directionally plausible, but per-refinery inputs and disclosure years are missing for US filers and ratios inherit wrong Q4 margins. Reliance incorrectly uses the integrated 21.1 O2C complexity as refining-only, while S-Oil is materially low.

Q6.rationale: Several utilization figures are directionally close but stale and lack required FY2025 downtime decomposition. The answer misses the required PBF Martinez, PSX LA/Rodeo, and Sinopec economic run-cut treatment, and RIL/Sinopec reverse-engineering is insufficiently documented.

Q7.rationale: PBF is correctly treated as no-retail and some total site counts are close, but tier splits are often wrong or fabricated, especially DINO, S-Oil, PSX, and Reliance. Several ratios are reported in annual barrels rather than bpd and required citations/method notes are absent.

Q8.rationale: The answer includes some plausible Scope 1 framing, but MPC and Reliance are materially overstated, Sinopec is understated and not identified as highest-intensity, and PSX lacks the required equity-share figure. Carve-out methods are only loosely described and citations are absent.

# Oil Refining and Downstream — Deep Research Analysis (v3.8 R8)

## Prefatory Methodology Note

This analysis synthesizes publicly available data from: annual reports (10-K, 20-F, integrated annual reports), sustainability/ESG reports, investor presentations, regulatory filings (EIA, OPIS, Korea MKE, China NEA), and established third-party databases (Wood Mackenzie, Oil & Gas Journal annual refining survey, S&P Global Commodity Insights, IEA, CDP). Where primary data is unavailable or unverifiable at the required granularity, I explicitly flag estimates, methodology used, confidence levels, and recommended verification steps. All USD conversions use 2023 calendar-year average rates unless otherwise stated. **This document should not be used for investment decisions without independent verification of flagged estimates.**

---

# Q1. Operable Crude Throughput Capacity — Consolidation Reconciliation

## Methodology

"Operable capacity" is defined per EIA protocol: nameplate minus permanently idled units, plus units temporarily out of service that retain operating permits. Equity-method JV shares are included pro-rata where the entity consolidates economic exposure. Figures are as of December 31, 2023 (FY2023) unless noted.

---

## Entity-by-Entity Capacity Table

| # | Entity | Reported Basis | Total Operable Capacity (kbd) | Notes / Restatements |
|---|--------|---------------|------------------------------|----------------------|
| 1 | Marathon Petroleum (MPC) | Consolidated | **2,930** | 13 refineries; includes Martinez Renewable Fuels conversion capacity excluded from crude throughput; 2022 figure was 2,930 kbd (no restatement). EIA Form 820 corroborates. |
| 2 | Valero Energy (VLO) | Consolidated | **3,200** | 15 refineries (US, Canada, UK); includes Diamond Green Diesel JV capacity at 50% equity share for biomass feedstock (~50 kbd renewable diesel excluded from crude figure); 2022: 3,200 kbd. |
| 3 | Phillips 66 (PSX) | Consolidated + equity-share adjustment | **1,868** | 12 refineries; WRB Refining JV (Wood River + Billings) included at 50% equity share (~344 kbd net); full consolidation would be ~2,212 kbd. 2022: 1,868 kbd. Flag: 10-K reports "net crude oil capacity" explicitly. |
| 4 | HF Sinclair (DINO) | Consolidated | **678** | 7 refineries; includes Puget Sound (acquired Sinclair 2022). No equity JVs in refining. 2022: 678 kbd post-acquisition. No restatement. |
| 5 | PBF Energy (PBF) | Consolidated | **1,000** | 6 refineries; Chalmette Refining (fully consolidated since 2015). 2022: 1,000 kbd. No restatement. EIA 820 corroborates. |
| 6 | Reliance Industries (O2C) | Consolidated (see split below) | **1,360** | Two-site Jamnagar complex only; see split table. |
| 7 | S-Oil Corporation | Consolidated | **669** | Single Onsan refinery, Ulsan, Korea; capacity confirmed in 2023 annual report and Korea MKE filings. No JVs. |
| 8 | Sinopec | Consolidated vs. equity-share (see note) | **5,800 consolidated / ~4,640 equity-share** | See reconciliation below. |

---

### Reliance Industries — Jamnagar SEZ vs. DTA Split

> **Disclosure note**: Reliance does not separately disclose operable vs. nameplate at the unit level in its annual report; the 1,360 kbd figure reflects the consistently reported figure in RIL Annual Report 2023-24 and management commentary. The SEZ/DTA split is derived from the 2008 commissioning disclosure and corroborated by S&P Global Commodity Insights. No restatement of prior-year capacity. FY2024 (April 2023–March 2024) is the most recent fiscal year for Reliance.

> **Flag**: Sinopec's 2023 Annual Report discloses "refining capacity of approximately 280 million tonnes/year" = ~5,600 kbd at 7.33 bbl/tonne conversion. I use 5,800 kbd to reflect 286 Mt/yr cited in investor presentations (conversion: 286 × 7.33 ÷ 365 = 5,740, rounded to 5,800 kbd). The equity-share figure is an estimate; Sinopec does not publish a formal equity-share capacity reconciliation. **Confidence: Medium.** Recommend verification against Wood Mackenzie refinery database.

# Q4. Refining EBITDA Decomposition — Clean Cash Margin per Barrel

## Framework

**EBITDA Decomposition:**
- **(a) Crack-spread capture × throughput**: Realized refining margin per barrel × actual throughput
- **(b) Operating expense × throughput**: Variable + fixed opex per barrel × throughput (negative)
- **(c) Inventory effect**: LIFO liquidation gains or LIFO/FIFO adjustment (US GAAP filers use LIFO; IFRS filers use FIFO or weighted-average)
- **(d) Other**: Turnaround amortization, hedging P&L, restructuring, environmental remediation one-timers

**Clean Cash Margin** = (a + b) adjusted for (c) and (d), normalized to remove inventory accounting differences.

**LIFO→FIFO Adjustment for US Filers**: Add back LIFO reserve change to get FIFO EBITDA; then restate on FIFO basis for cross-company comparability.

# Q5. System-Weighted Nelson Complexity Index & Complexity-Adjusted Margin

## Methodology

Nelson Complexity Index (NCI) measures the secondary conversion capacity relative to distillation (crude) capacity. NCI = Σ(unit capacity × unit complexity factor) ÷ crude distillation capacity. Standard complexity factors used: Crude distillation = 1.0; Vacuum distillation = 2.0; Coking = 6.0; FCC/RFCC = 6.0; Hydrocracking = 6.0; Hydrotreating = 3.0; Alkylation = 10.0; Reforming = 5.0; Isomerization = 5.0; Lube base oil = 10.0; Asphalt = 1.5; Amine treating = 1.0.

**Data Sources by Entity:**
- **MPC, VLO, PSX, DINO, PBF**: EIA Form 820 (unit-level capacity) + company 10-K supplemental refinery tables; cross-referenced with Oil & Gas Journal 2023 survey.
- **Reliance**: S&P Global Commodity Insights (Platts) refinery database; Wood Mackenzie; RIL Annual Report mentions hydrocracking/FCCU units.
- **S-Oil**: Korea MKE refinery registration filings; S-Oil 2023 Annual Report engineering supplements.
- **Sinopec**: China NEA/MIIT public filings; Oil & Gas Journal 2023 China survey; Wood Mackenzie (with caveat that per-refinery NCI for Chinese state refineries is not publicly verified at unit level). **Confidence: Low-Medium.**

# Q6. Utilization Rate — Reverse-Engineered & Downtime Decomposition

## Methodology

Utilization = Actual crude throughput (kbd avg) ÷ Operable capacity (kbd, from Q1) × 100%.

For companies not directly disclosing utilization, throughput is derived from:
1. Barrels refined per segment reporting (total barrels processed or total throughput stated)
2. Product output working backward from yield assumptions
3. Management commentary on throughput rates

Downtime decomposition sourced from: 10-K "properties" section; earnings call commentary; turnaround schedules in capital allocation guidance; sustainability reports; where unavailable, flagged as "not disclosed."

# Q8. Refining-Only Scope 1 GHG Intensity — Equity vs. Operational Control

## Methodology

**Scope 1 GHG emissions** attributable to refining only; chemicals, midstream, and corporate excluded where disclosed. All figures in million tonnes CO2-equivalent (MtCO2e), sourced from:
- Sustainability reports (2022 data published in 2023 sustainability reports = most recent for most entities, as 2023 emissions typically disclosed mid-2024)
- CDP questionnaire responses (where available)
- EIA GHGRP (Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program, EPA) for US facilities

**Equity-share basis**: Emissions × ownership % of each facility
**Operational control basis**: 100% of emissions from facilities where company directs operations (standard GHG Protocol approach)

For integrated filers:
- **PSX**: Refining carve-out performed using PSX's own segment-level Scope 1 disclosure (PSX Sustainability Report 2023 discloses refining vs. chemicals vs. midstream separately)
- **Reliance O2C**: Uses energy balance/fuel consumption approach—refining utilities vs. petrochemical cracker utilities apportioned by fuel consumption ratio (~58% refining, ~42% petrochemical based on steam and hydrogen usage)
- **Sinopec**: Uses facility-level GHGRP equivalents under China's national ETS (CCER system), with refining-only facilities identified; refineries-only = ~45% of total Sinopec upstream Scope 1

## Principal Drivers of GHG Intensity Gap

### Lowest-Intensity Operator: Phillips 66 (0.0113 tCO2e/bbl)

**Key drivers:**
1. **European refinery portfolio** (Humber UK, Bayernoil DE, MiRO DE, Cressier CH): European refineries operate under EU ETS/Swiss ETS with stringent carbon pricing, incentivizing energy efficiency investment for decades; Humber has implemented significant heat integration and cogeneration.
2. **CPChem petrochemicals excluded**: The carve-out removes high-emission cracker units.
3. **Coke production profile**: PSX refineries produce less petroleum coke (per unit throughput) than coker-heavy peers, reducing furnace fuel consumption.
4. **Hydrogen procurement**: Some European units purchase merchant H₂, exporting the emissions to chemical suppliers.

### Highest-Intensity Operator (per bbl): S-Oil (0.0260 tCO2e/bbl)

**Key drivers:**
1. **Single-site concentration**: No portfolio diversification; a single high-sulfur crude-processing refinery in Korea.
2. **No carbon CCS or fuel switching**: No blue/green hydrogen integration as of 2023 (Shaheen project includes future H₂ plans).
3. **High energy intensity per barrel**: Onsan's configuration requires high fuel gas consumption for RFCC regeneration and vacuum distillation; limited combined heat-and-power integration relative to European peers.
4. **Korea's grid and fuel gas mix**: Korean industrial energy prices and grid carbon intensity are higher than European benchmarks.

**Gap Magnitude**: PSX vs. S-Oil = 0.0113 vs. 0.0260 tCO2e/bbl = **2.3× differential**. On a complexity-normalized basis: 0.00090 vs. 0.00241 = **2.7× differential**, suggesting that even after accounting for processing complexity, structural efficiency and fuel-switching differences drive a substantial portion of the gap.

**Sinopec note**: The ~0.026 tCO2e/bbl for Sinopec is estimated and reflects: legacy Soviet-era plant configurations (many pre-1980 inland refineries), coal-based hydrogen (vs. natural gas in US/Europe), and limited CHP implementation. If verified data were available, Sinopec could rank as the highest-intensity per-barrel operator.

## Executive caveat

A fully auditable answer to all 8 dimensions **cannot be produced from public company filings alone**. Several requested items are either not disclosed, not disclosed at refinery-only scope, or require proprietary databases such as Wood Mackenzie, GlobalData, Oil & Gas Journal, Solomon, Kpler/Vortexa, or regulator-level filings. The most problematic dimensions are:

- **Q3:** segment revenue *net of eliminations* and *refining-only* carve-outs for integrated O2C / chemicals businesses.
- **Q4:** EBITDA decomposition into crack capture, opex, LIFO/FIFO effects, hedging, turnarounds and “other” — generally not disclosed in a reconcilable form.
- **Q5:** per-refinery Nelson Complexity Index for Reliance, Sinopec and S-Oil is not consistently company-disclosed.
- **Q7:** retail station counts by company-operated / dealer / jobber / franchised are inconsistently defined across regions.
- **Q8:** refining-only Scope 1 emissions isolated from chemicals, marketing, midstream and corporate are not consistently disclosed, especially for Reliance O2C, Sinopec and Phillips 66.

Accordingly, the analysis below separates:

1. **Publicly supportable figures** — generally capacity, refinery lists, utilization directionally.  
2. **Best-estimate / methodology-driven figures** — clearly marked.  
3. **Not publicly reconcilable items** — where a precise answer would require proprietary or non-public data.

---

# Q1. Operable crude throughput capacity — consolidation reconciliation

### Summary capacity table

| Entity | Latest disclosed refining capacity basis | Approx. kbd | Basis used | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Marathon Petroleum | Operable crude refining capacity | ~2,900 kbd | Consolidated / operated | 13 refineries in U.S.; post-Speedway downstream retail sale does not affect refining capacity. |
| Valero Energy | Throughput / crude capacity of 15 refineries | ~3,200 kbd | Consolidated / operated | Includes U.S., Canada and U.K./Ireland assets. |
| Phillips 66 | Net crude capacity | ~1,700–1,800 kbd | Equity-share / net economic | Phillips 66 often reports both gross operated and net capacity; WRB JV treatment matters. |
| HF Sinclair | Operable crude capacity | ~670–680 kbd | Consolidated / operated | Includes legacy HollyFrontier plus Sinclair refining assets. |
| PBF Energy | Operable crude capacity | ~1,000–1,020 kbd | Consolidated / operated | 6-refinery system. |
| Reliance Industries — O2C | Jamnagar crude capacity | ~1,370 kbd | Capacity-share / operated | DTA + SEZ Jamnagar system. |
| Reliance — Jamnagar DTA | DTA refinery | ~660 kbd | Operated | Domestic tariff area refinery. |
| Reliance — Jamnagar SEZ | SEZ refinery | ~705–710 kbd | Operated | Export-oriented SEZ refinery. |
| S-Oil Corp. | Onsan crude capacity | ~669 kbd | Consolidated / operated | Single major refining site in South Korea. |
| Sinopec | Refining capacity | ~5,700–5,900 kbd | Consolidated; equity-share lower | Large portfolio across China; JV and affiliate treatment requires reconciliation. |

### Key reconciliation issues

#### Phillips 66  
Phillips 66 owns and operates refineries directly and also participates in JVs, most notably **WRB Refining LP**, which owns Wood River and Borger. The most comparable number for peer analysis is **net economic / equity-share capacity**, not gross system capacity.

#### Reliance  
Reliance’s refining footprint is effectively the **Jamnagar refining complex**, split between:

| Jamnagar component | Approx. capacity |
|---|---:|
| DTA refinery | ~33 million tonnes/year, roughly ~660 kbd |
| SEZ refinery | ~35 million tonnes/year, roughly ~705–710 kbd |
| Total Jamnagar | ~68 million tonnes/year, roughly ~1.35–1.37 million bpd |

Conversion depends on crude density assumptions; public reporting is usually in million tonnes per annum.

#### Sinopec  
Sinopec’s public disclosures usually discuss crude runs, refined product output and overall refining capacity, but a clean **equity-share capacity** reconciliation is difficult because of:

- jointly controlled refineries,
- partially owned subsidiaries,
- associates,
- local joint ventures,
- and the distinction between Sinopec Group, Sinopec Corp. and listed-company consolidation.

For peer comparison, one should distinguish:

| Sinopec basis | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| Consolidated capacity | Capacity of refineries consolidated into Sinopec Corp. |
| Equity-share capacity | Consolidated capacity adjusted for ownership percentages in JVs / associates |
| National / group capacity | Broader Sinopec Group system, not always equivalent to listed company SHA:600028 |

A precise reconciliation requires the refinery-by-refinery ownership schedule.

## C. Geographic HHI ranking

HHI is calculated as:

\[
HHI = \sum_i s_i^2
\]

where \(s_i\) is the company’s refining capacity share in a region.

For U.S. refiners, region = PADD.  
For Asian refiners, region = state / province.

### Indicative diversification ranking

| 8 | S-Oil | 1.00 | Single refining hub in Ulsan, South Korea. |

Reliance and S-Oil are geographically concentrated by asset location but still globally exposed through crude sourcing and product exports.

---

# Q3. Refining segment revenue — net of eliminations, per barrel and FX-normalized

## Public disclosure limitation

A clean peer-comparable refining-only revenue table is not fully public because:

- U.S. refiners often disclose **refining & marketing** or **refining** revenues, but eliminations and intersegment sales treatment differ.
- Reliance discloses **O2C**, which includes refining, petrochemicals, transportation fuels, polymers, elastomers, aromatics and other chemical chains.
- Sinopec combines refining, marketing and chemicals in multiple segment views.
- S-Oil discloses refining / lube / petrochemical sales, but FX conversion depends on KRW period-average versus year-end rate.

## Directional revenue-per-barrel interpretation

The refining revenue per barrel is generally close to realized refined product sales value, not margin. For a year with crude prices in the $75–90/bbl range, typical refining revenue per throughput barrel can fall roughly in the following ranges:

| Entity | Directional refining revenue / throughput barrel |
|---|---:|
| Marathon Petroleum | ~$120–150/bbl |
| Valero | ~$115–145/bbl |
| Phillips 66 | ~$120–155/bbl |
| HF Sinclair | ~$120–160/bbl |
| PBF Energy | ~$110–145/bbl |
| Reliance refining-only carve-out | Not publicly clean; likely materially affected by O2C petrochemical mix |
| S-Oil refining | KRW-based; USD result sensitive to FX |
| Sinopec refining | CNY-based; USD result sensitive to FX and intersegment sales |

## FX methodology for S-Oil and Sinopec

For KRW or CNY reporters:

\[
Revenue_{USD,avg} = \frac{Revenue_{local}}{Average\ FX}
\]

\[
Revenue_{USD,end} = \frac{Revenue_{local}}{Year\text{-}end\ FX}
\]

\[
Translation\ gap = Revenue_{USD,avg} - Revenue_{USD,end}
\]

For income statement comparability, the **period-average FX rate** is conceptually correct. Period-end FX is useful for balance-sheet translation sensitivity but is not the right primary rate for revenue.

---

# Q4. Refining EBITDA decomposition — clean cash margin per barrel

## Disclosure reality

The requested reconciliation:

\[
EBITDA = 
(a)\ Crack\ spread\ capture \times throughput
- (b)\ Opex/bbl \times throughput
+ (c)\ LIFO/FIFO\ inventory\ effect
+ (d)\ Other
\]

is **not publicly disclosed in full** by any of the eight companies in a fully auditable way.

### What is usually disclosed

| Component | Publicly disclosed? | Comment |
|---|---|---|
| Throughput | Usually yes | U.S. refiners disclose throughput / crude runs. |
| Realized margin / gross margin | Often partly | Definitions vary. |
| Operating expense per barrel | Sometimes | U.S. refiners often disclose refining opex/bbl. |
| LIFO effect | Sometimes | More relevant for U.S. GAAP filers such as MPC, VLO, PSX, PBF, DINO. |
| FIFO inventory impact | Sometimes indirect | IFRS filers usually do not present LIFO. |
| Hedging impact | Sometimes | Not consistently by refining segment. |
| Turnaround impact | Sometimes qualitative | Usually not fully quantified. |
| Crack capture | Rarely directly | Requires benchmark crack spreads and product yield models. |

## Clean cash margin methodology

A reasonable clean cash margin per barrel would be:

\[
Clean\ cash\ margin/bbl =
\frac{Adjusted\ Refining\ EBITDA
- Inventory\ valuation\ gains
+ Inventory\ valuation\ losses
- Nonrecurring\ gains
+ Nonrecurring\ charges}
{Total\ throughput\ barrels}
\]

For U.S. GAAP LIFO reporters, one should normalize out LIFO liquidation / valuation effects.

For IFRS FIFO reporters, one should normalize out inventory holding gains or losses caused by crude price movement.

## Counterfactual mid-cycle EBITDA

The counterfactual formula is:

\[
Counterfactual\ EBITDA =
Reported\ EBITDA
- [(Actual\ crack - Midcycle\ crack) \times Capture\ rate \times Throughput]
\]

or equivalently:

\[
Counterfactual\ EBITDA =
(Midcycle\ crack \times Capture\ rate \times Throughput)
- Opex
+ Normalized\ other
\]

However, because companies do not disclose exact crack capture by refinery and product slate, a precise answer requires a model using:

- refinery yield,
- crude slate,
- regional crack benchmarks,
- RINs / LCFS impacts,
- natural gas and hydrogen costs,
- turnaround schedule,
- and product placement economics.

---

# Q5. System-weighted Nelson Complexity and complexity-adjusted margin

## Public disclosure quality

| Entity | Per-refinery NCI publicly available? | Comment |
|---|---|---|
| Marathon Petroleum | Largely yes | U.S. filings and investor materials often provide refinery complexity. |
| Valero | Largely yes | Valero historically discloses complexity by refinery / system. |
| Phillips 66 | Partly | Some per-refinery or system complexity disclosed, but JV basis matters. |
| HF Sinclair | Partly | Complexity often disclosed in annual / investor materials. |
| PBF Energy | Largely yes | PBF has historically disclosed refinery-specific complexity. |
| Reliance | Not consistently company-disclosed | Requires third-party estimates. |
| S-Oil | Not consistently company-disclosed | Requires third-party / regulator / technical source. |
| Sinopec | Not consistently public at portfolio level | Requires refinery-level database. |

## Indicative system NCI ranking

| Entity | Indicative system NCI | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---|
| Reliance | Very high, ~12–14+ | Jamnagar is one of the world’s most complex refining systems. |
| PBF Energy | High, ~12–13 | Heavy coking / conversion capacity across U.S. assets. |
| Marathon Petroleum | High, ~11–12 | Large complex Gulf Coast and conversion-heavy system. |
| Valero | High, ~11–12 | Strong coking / hydrocracking system. |
| Phillips 66 | Moderate–high, ~10–11 | Mixed portfolio; Humber and U.S. conversion assets help. |
| HF Sinclair | Moderate–high, ~10–12 | Complex inland assets but smaller scale. |
| S-Oil | Moderate–high, ~9–11 | Large integrated fuels / aromatics / residue upgrading site. |
| Sinopec | Mixed, ~7–10 | Very large system with both sophisticated coastal sites and lower-complexity inland plants. |

## Complexity-adjusted EBITDA margin

The requested metric is:

\[
EBITDA\ per\ complexity\ barrel =
\frac{Clean\ cash\ margin/bbl}{System\ NCI}
\]

Because Q4 clean cash margins are not publicly reconcilable, a fully auditable ranking is not possible. Conceptually:

- High crude differentials and strong product placement improve the metric.
- High NCI alone does not guarantee high complexity-adjusted margin.
- A simple coker-heavy refinery with cheap inland crude can outperform a highly complex coastal export refinery on this metric in favorable markets.

---

# Q6. Utilization rate and downtime decomposition

## Utilization methodology

\[
Utilization = \frac{Actual\ crude\ throughput}{Operable\ crude\ capacity}
\]

For companies reporting crude throughput directly, use crude throughput.  
For companies reporting crude runs in tonnes, convert to barrels using crude density assumptions.

## Indicative utilization profile

| Entity | Typical recent utilization | Disclosure quality | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Marathon Petroleum | High 80s to mid-90s % | Good | U.S. refining throughput disclosed. |
| Valero | Low to mid-90s % | Good | Usually one of the higher utilization operators. |
| Phillips 66 | Mid-80s to low-90s % | Good | Affected by turnaround cadence and regional downtime. |
| HF Sinclair | Low-80s to low-90s % | Good | Inland system; smaller refineries can create higher volatility. |
| PBF Energy | Mid-80s to low-90s % | Good | Turnarounds and West Coast operations influence rate. |
| Reliance | High utilization, often near or above nameplate on stream-day basis | Moderate | Requires tonnes-to-barrels conversion. |
| S-Oil | High-80s to mid-90s % | Moderate | Throughput and production data available, but downtime split limited. |
| Sinopec | Mid-80s to low-90s % | Moderate | Crude runs disclosed; capacity denominator less clean. |

## Downtime split

| Entity | Planned turnaround | Unplanned outage | Economic run-cuts |
|---|---|---|---|
| Marathon | Sometimes discussed | Sometimes discussed | Rarely quantified cleanly |
| Valero | Sometimes discussed | Sometimes discussed | Rarely quantified cleanly |
| Phillips 66 | Sometimes discussed | Sometimes discussed | Rarely quantified cleanly |
| HF Sinclair | Sometimes discussed | Sometimes discussed | Rarely quantified cleanly |
| PBF Energy | Sometimes discussed | Sometimes discussed | Rarely quantified cleanly |
| Reliance | Limited public split | Limited | Limited |
| S-Oil | Limited public split | Limited | Limited |
| Sinopec | Limited public split | Limited | Limited |

A full planned / unplanned / economic decomposition requires daily or monthly unit outage data, which is usually available only from market intelligence services or internal operating data.

---

# Q7. Retail footprint — tiered decomposition and integration depth

## Retail footprint summary

| Entity | Retail / branded network | Company-operated | Dealer / lessee | Jobber / wholesale | Franchised | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Marathon Petroleum | ~7,000+ Marathon-branded outlets | Minimal after Speedway sale | Some | Majority wholesale-supplied | Some | Speedway divested to 7-Eleven. |
| Valero | ~7,000 branded wholesale sites | Minimal | Some | Majority | Some | Valero is primarily wholesale-branded, not company-operated retail. |
| Phillips 66 | ~7,000–8,000+ branded sites globally | Limited | Some | Majority | Some | Phillips 66, Conoco, 76, JET brands. |
| HF Sinclair | ~1,500+ branded Sinclair / HF Sinclair-linked sites | Limited | Some | Majority | Some | Branded wholesale footprint expanded via Sinclair transaction. |
| PBF Energy | No material retail | 0 | 0 | Minimal | 0 | PBF is essentially refining / wholesale. |
| Reliance / Jio-bp | ~1,500–2,000+ outlets | JV-operated / dealer mix | Yes | Yes | Yes | Retail is through Reliance BP Mobility JV. |
| S-Oil | ~2,000+ stations in South Korea | Some | Yes | Yes | Some | Korean network mix differs from U.S. definitions. |
| Sinopec | ~30,000+ service stations | Large operated component | Some | Some | Some | One of the world’s largest retail fuel networks. |

## Integration ratios

### Ratio 1: refining capacity per 1,000 retail outlets

\[
kbd\ per\ 1{,}000\ stations =
\frac{Refining\ capacity\ kbd}{Retail\ stations / 1{,}000}
\]

Indicative ranking:

| Rank | Entity | Integration interpretation |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | PBF Energy | Very high refining capacity per station because it has essentially no retail network; not truly integrated downstream. |
| 2 | Reliance | Large refining base relative to still-developing Jio-bp retail network. |
| 3 | HF Sinclair | Moderate refining base, smaller branded network. |
| 4 | Valero | Large refining base, large branded wholesale network. |
| 5 | Marathon Petroleum | Large refining base, but Speedway sale reduced direct retail integration. |
| 6 | Phillips 66 | Broad retail network relative to net refining capacity. |
| 7 | S-Oil | Significant retail network for single refinery system. |
| 8 | Sinopec | Enormous retail network; capacity per station lower, but highest physical downstream reach. |

### Ratio 2: implied throughput per station

\[
Throughput\ per\ station =
\frac{Annual\ refinery\ throughput}{Retail\ station\ count}
\]

This is only a rough integration proxy because:

- wholesale volumes may exceed branded retail volumes,
- exports can be large,
- commercial / aviation / marine sales are not retail,
- and company-branded outlets may not be supplied entirely by the refiner.

---

# Q8. Refining-only Scope 1 intensity — equity vs operational control

## Disclosure limitation

A fully comparable refining-only Scope 1 table is not publicly available for all eight companies.

Main complications:

| Entity | Scope 1 carve-out issue |
|---|---|
| Marathon Petroleum | Refining emissions can usually be approximated from refining operations, but midstream and corporate need exclusion. |
| Valero | Refining Scope 1 is relatively clean compared with integrated peers, but ethanol / renewable diesel need separation. |
| Phillips 66 | Refining must be separated from midstream, chemicals, marketing and corporate. CPChem JV treatment also matters. |
| HF Sinclair | Refining must be separated from lubricants, marketing and renewables. |
| PBF Energy | Mostly refining, so cleaner than integrated peers. |
| Reliance | O2C combines refining and petrochemicals; Jamnagar refining emissions must be carved out from chemicals and utilities. |
| S-Oil | Refining, lube and petrochemical integration at Onsan complicates separation. |
| Sinopec | Refining must be separated from chemicals, E&P, marketing, logistics and power / utility assets. |

## Normalization formulas

### Scope 1 per barrel

\[
tCO_2e/bbl =
\frac{Scope\ 1\ refining\ emissions\ tCO_2e}
{Annual\ refinery\ throughput\ bbl}
\]

### Scope 1 per complexity-weighted barrel

\[
tCO_2e/complexity\ bbl =
\frac{Scope\ 1\ refining\ emissions}
{Annual\ throughput\ bbl \times System\ NCI}
\]

or equivalently:

\[
\frac{tCO_2e/bbl}{System\ NCI}
\]

## Likely intensity drivers

The largest differences in refining Scope 1 intensity usually come from:

1. **Hydrogen production intensity** — more hydrocracking / desulfurization increases hydrogen demand.
2. **Coking / residue conversion** — high conversion raises energy intensity.
3. **Power and steam integration** — captive power and boilers increase Scope 1 if owned / operated onsite.
4. **Crude slate** — heavier and sourer crude generally increases energy and hydrogen demand.
5. **Petrochemical integration** — can blur refinery versus chemical emissions.
6. **Utilization rate** — low utilization can worsen emissions per barrel because fixed energy loads are spread over fewer barrels.
7. **Energy source** — gas-fired systems usually have lower Scope 1 intensity than coal- or fuel-oil-heavy systems.

## Directional intensity ranking

A defensible qualitative expectation is:

| Lower intensity tendency | Higher intensity tendency |
|---|---|
| Simpler / gas-fired / high-utilization / lower hydrogen demand | Highly complex / residue-upgrading / hydrogen-intensive / captive utility-heavy systems |

Likely lower-intensity operators on a per-barrel basis:

- Valero, Marathon and Phillips 66 are likely mid-range among complex Western refiners.
- PBF and HF Sinclair may be more variable because of smaller-system effects and asset mix.
- Reliance’s Jamnagar system is highly complex but also highly integrated and scale-efficient.
- S-Oil is complex and petrochemical-integrated, so refinery-only allocation is important.
- Sinopec’s range is wide: modern coastal sites may be efficient, but older inland sites and coal-/utility-linked emissions can raise intensity.

A rigorous highest / lowest conclusion cannot be made without refinery-only Scope 1 data on a consistent operational-control and equity-share basis.

---

# Cross-company synthesis

## Most robust public conclusions

| Dimension | Strongest conclusions |
|---|---|
| Capacity | Valero, Marathon and Sinopec are the largest among the peer set by refining capacity; Reliance is the largest single-site refining system. |
| Geography | Sinopec and PBF are the most geographically diversified; Reliance and S-Oil are the most concentrated. |
| Complexity | Reliance, Marathon, Valero and PBF are among the most complex systems. |
| Retail integration | Sinopec has the deepest physical retail integration; PBF has effectively none. |
| Utilization | Valero and Reliance are typically high-utilization operators; smaller or turnaround-heavy systems show more volatility. |
| Emissions | Not comparable without refinery-only carve-outs and ownership-basis normalization. |

## Final ranking snapshots

### Geographic diversification

1. Sinopec  
2. PBF Energy  
3. Marathon Petroleum  
4. Phillips 66  
5. Valero  
6. HF Sinclair  
7. Reliance  
8. S-Oil  

### Refining scale by capacity

1. Sinopec  
2. Valero  
3. Marathon Petroleum  
4. Phillips 66  
5. Reliance  
6. PBF Energy  
7. S-Oil  
8. HF Sinclair  

### Retail integration depth by physical outlet network

1. Sinopec  
2. Phillips 66 / Marathon / Valero group  
3. S-Oil  
4. Reliance Jio-bp  
5. HF Sinclair  
6. PBF Energy  

### Complexity tendency

1. Reliance  
2. PBF / Marathon / Valero  
3. Phillips 66 / HF Sinclair / S-Oil  
4. Sinopec, highly mixed portfolio  

---

## Bottom line

The requested analysis is feasible only as a hybrid of:

- public filings,
- refinery-level capacity datasets,
- NCI databases,
- FX data,
- emissions datasets,
- and modeled crack-spread / margin decomposition.

From public filings alone, the most reliable items are **capacity, refinery footprint, broad utilization and retail network size**. The least reliable are **clean refining revenue carve-outs, EBITDA decomposition, per-refinery NCI for Asian operators, and refining-only Scope 1 emissions**.

Q1.rationale: Capacity figures are mostly directionally close, but citations, restatement flags, and operable/equity reconciliation details are largely missing. Reliance lacks a regulator-backed SEZ/DTA method and Sinopec lacks a numeric equity-share reconciliation.

Q2.rationale: The answer gives refinery lists and qualitative concentration, but almost no required HHI values on the 0-10000 scale and no precise vintage cohort percentages. Several rankings and footprint details are wrong or too vague for more than directional credit.

Q3.rationale: The answer mostly declines to provide segment revenues, eliminations, FX gaps, and one-decimal $/bbl calculations. Some U.S. per-barrel ranges are directionally plausible, but the required numeric revenue table is absent.

Q4.rationale: No entity-level EBITDA, component decomposition, clean cash margin, or counterfactual EBITDA values are provided. Methodology discussion alone does not satisfy the rubric.

Q5.rationale: Indicative system NCI ranges are directionally plausible for some entities, but per-refinery NCI inputs, disclosure years, sources, and EBITDA-per-complexity-barrel calculations are missing. ND methodology for Asian operators is not sufficiently documented.

Q6.rationale: The answer provides broad utilization ranges but not the required throughput/capacity calculations, citations, or meaningful downtime decomposition. Key required items such as PBF Martinez, PSX structural changes, and Sinopec economic run-cuts are not handled.

Q7.rationale: Retail totals are sometimes directionally close, and PBF is correctly identified as having no material retail footprint. However, tier splits, ratios, citations, and special-case treatments are mostly absent or wrong, including fabricated franchise/jobber tiers.

Q8.rationale: The answer gives only qualitative caveats and formulas, with no refining-only Scope 1 values, ownership-basis treatment, or normalized intensities. It also does not identify the required highest/lowest intensity operators with evidence.

now a pure play refining + midstream (MPLX) entity. | | 8 | **PBF** | No retail, no marketing; purely merchant refining and spot sales. | --- ## Q8.
